name: Govern the agent
note: When the AI runs across many files, you can't read every line — so you govern differently. Pick the move that keeps an agentic change accountable.

items.prompt: You need an agent to migrate 30 call-sites to a new API. Best first move?
candidates: Have it do one representative call-site end-to-end, review and verify that, then let it batch the rest against the verified pattern — gate the pattern before it's applied 30 times
Let it do all 30 at once and review the final diff — fastest
Do all 30 by hand; agents can't be trusted with migrations
Let it run and only check that the tests pass at the end
items.correct: Have it do one representative call-site end-to-end, review and verify that, then let it batch the rest against the verified pattern — gate the pattern before it's applied 30 times
items.explanation: Gating the pattern on one unit before fanning out catches a systematic error 30x cheaper, while reviewing 30 files at once is exactly where comprehension collapses.
items.principle: Verify the pattern on one unit before the agent applies it to many.

items.prompt: Mid-refactor, the agent proposes to also 'clean up' unrelated code it noticed. Right move?
candidates: Hold it to scope: 'stay within the auth refactor; list the other cleanups separately and I'll decide' — uncontrolled scope creep is where agent changes become unreviewable
Let it — more cleanup is always good
Let it, as long as the tests still pass afterward
Abandon the agent and start the whole thing over manually
items.correct: Hold it to scope: 'stay within the auth refactor; list the other cleanups separately and I'll decide' — uncontrolled scope creep is where agent changes become unreviewable
items.explanation: Scope discipline at checkpoints keeps the change reviewable and the preregistration meaningful. Letting an agent expand scope is how you end with files you can't account for.
items.principle: Hold the agent to the scope you committed; surface extras, don't absorb them.

items.prompt: An agent changed 14 files; you can't carefully read all of them. How do you govern it?
candidates: Read the seams (the changed interfaces/contracts) deeply, run the preregistered gate over the whole change, and deep-read the 2–3 riskiest files while sampling the rest — govern by contract + gate + risk-weighted reading
Read all 14 files line by line, however long it takes
Trust it if the tests pass — that's what tests are for
Reject the whole change because you can't read all of it
items.correct: Read the seams (the changed interfaces/contracts) deeply, run the preregistered gate over the whole change, and deep-read the 2–3 riskiest files while sampling the rest — govern by contract + gate + risk-weighted reading
items.explanation: At scale you govern by interfaces, the gate, and risk-weighted sampling — the senior real-world practice. Reading everything doesn't scale; trusting tests alone misses what they don't cover.
items.principle: When you can't read every line, govern the seams, the gate, and the riskiest units.
